inline.s: Ordinary people cannot be without thought. If they are not mindful of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, they will surely be mindful of greed, anger, and delusion. Being mindful of greed, anger, and delusion, evil karma such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct arises in swarms, and the wheel of birth and death has no rest. The Buddha, therefore, following the situation and leading it along, seized on the habit of living beings that they cannot be without thought, and skillfully and expediently used a single thought of the Buddha to substitute for false thoughts, causing living beings to turn false thoughts into thoughts of the Buddha and to exchange the defiled mind for a pure mind, and thereby easily to be reborn in the Pure Land and escape from birth and death. Great Master Chewu says:

"The essential of purifying the mind is nothing other than Buddha-recitation. One thought in accord is one thought of Buddha; thought after thought in accord is thought after thought of Buddha. A clear pearl
(a precious pearl that clarifies turbid water)
cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear; the Buddha-name cast into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot but become Buddha."

(From the Collected Works of Great Master Chewu.) Therefore, Buddha-recitation is precisely the most intimate and simplest transformation made at the very place closest to a living being's birth and death. And the key to this transformation is:
awareness.
Be aware thought after thought: the moment a false thought arises, immediately use the Buddha-name to turn it away.
One must genuinely and truly carry out this 'awareness
turn it away' practice, letting no single thought slip by, and seeing through each and every thought.
With long practice and deep merit, one naturally fuses into a single whole, subdues the afflictions, and accomplishes the pure karma. The key to purifying the mind is:
use the Buddha-name to turn away false thoughts.
[Awareness thought after thought] In reciting the Buddha-name, be aware of the present thought. See in detail
Aware Buddha-Recitation

the chapter 'Aware of the Present Thought.' [Not letting a single thought slip by] Every false thought, do not let it slide past unbeknownst to you. [Seeing through each thought] Every false thought, do not be enveloped by it, do not listen and follow its play, do not take it as a real matter, and above all do not be kidnapped by it.
To put an end to birth and death, one must know the root of birth and death, and how to uproot it. The patriarchs instruct:

The root of birth and death is precisely the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion; and to uproot the root of birth and death is precisely to spare no effort in the single transformation of a thought in this mind!

One must, amid the realms that appear in daily use, at the times when wife and children gather together, in the dealings among relatives and friends, at the places where right and profit, adverse and favorable, press upon one another, and before joy, anger, greed, and delusion have yet arisen, fix one's gaze and look intently beforehand, and truly, clearly see what is the root of birth and death, and immediately with all one's strength uproot it.
Question: May I practice breath Buddha-recitation while walking?

Answer: Yes. The method is: while walking, silently recite 'Amitabha Buddha,' one character for each step; four steps for an in-breath, four steps for an out-breath. This method, though excellent, is like riding a bicycle: there is a process of learning it, but once mastered, its benefit is inexhaustible. The breathing remains abdominal breathing: on the in-breath the abdomen protrudes, and on the out-breath the abdomen sinks in.
Question: I cannot sustain breath Buddha-recitation for long; after a while I feel tightness in the chest and shortness of breath, very uncomfortable. What should I do?

Answer: The key point of breath Buddha-recitation is to follow the breath. That is, follow the natural breathing and recite the Buddha-name, without controlling or changing the breath. The breathing during breath Buddha-recitation should be the same as your ordinary breathing when not reciting. What you need to do now is carefully come to understand how to follow the breath and recite, working on the word 'follow,' without controlling or changing the breath. First practice in a still state; when your skill in stillness is mature, then gradually practice it in movement.

Question: After practicing breath Buddha-recitation a long time, sometimes I feel the breath is not smooth. Later I used bulging the abdomen and tucking the abdomen to assist abdominal breathing: bulge the abdomen on the in-breath, tuck the abdomen on the out-breath. In this way I solved the problem of the unsmooth breath. May I practice breath Buddha-recitation in this way?
Answer: Yes, entirely.

Question: I have a weak digestive system, and found online that massaging the Sifeng acupoints, pinching the points with the tip of the thumb, can help. So while practicing breath Buddha-recitation, I also pinch the Sifeng acupoints. The method is: on the in-breath recite 'Ami' (Amita), and on the out-breath recite 'Tuofo' (-buddha), and pinch the acupoint on the out-breath; pinch one acupoint on each out-breath, pinching each acupoint five times, silently counting in the mind, and so on in rotation. (You may also do it with a single hand, using the thumb to pinch the Sifeng acupoints of the same hand.) After a period of time, the old ailment of my digestive system was cured, and I found that reciting the Buddha-name in this way not only gathers the mind and resists distraction, but is also easy to sustain. My question is: may I recite the Buddha-name in this way?

Answer: Your method is similar to pinching the prayer beads while reciting the Buddha-name; both are crutches, and help to gather the mind. The advantage of pinching acupoints is that it is not restricted by circumstances: in meetings, in conversation, while sleeping, and so on, it can all be done. If you feel it gathers the mind, resists distraction, and is easy to sustain (a Buddha-recitation method is good if it satisfies these three conditions), then of course you may recite the Buddha-name in this way. At the same time, you should put more effort into deep faith and resolute vows.

In response to fellow practitioners' request, the questioner answered: Let me describe the specific method I now use, of 'breath Buddha-recitation while also pinching the Sifeng acupoints,' for everyone's reference. The main points are three: first, the breathing remains abdominal breathing: on the in-breath the abdomen protrudes, and on the out-breath the abdomen sinks in. On the in-breath recite 'Ami,' and on the out-breath recite 'Tuofo.' Second, pinch the acupoints on the out-breath. With both hands, use each thumb to pinch the Sifeng acupoints of that same hand, pinching one acupoint on each out-breath and pinching each acupoint once, in order: index finger, middle finger, ring finger, little finger; little finger, ring finger, middle finger, index finger; index finger, middle finger, ring finger, little finger; and so on in this cycle. Third, at the same time, be focused and continuously aware of the Buddha-name, clearly knowing the thought-mark of the Buddha-name (how each character is produced), and whether there is only the thought of reciting the Buddha. I use this method whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; only when walking is it one character per step, four steps for an in-breath, four steps for an out-breath, while the method of pinching the acupoints and being aware of the Buddha-name remains unchanged.

Question: I tried the above acupoint-pinching method for a while and found it gathers the mind well. But since my digestive system has no ailment, doing this seems cumbersome. Is there a simpler method?

Answer: You may replace pinching the acupoints with the opening and closing of the palms, single hand or both hands. On the in-breath, the palm opens flat and the abdomen protrudes, reciting 'Ami'; on the out-breath, the palm closes and the abdomen sinks in, reciting 'Tuofo.' Once skilled, the opening and closing of the palms may be done slightly, so slightly that others will not notice; in short, what is comfortable, convenient, and sustainable is best. At the same time, be focused and continuously aware of the Buddha-name, clearly knowing the thought-mark of the Buddha-name (how each character is produced), and whether there is only the thought of reciting the Buddha.

Even so, whether pinching acupoints or opening and closing the palms, after all both are auxiliary movements. Once you have fully mastered breath Buddha-recitation, when you feel it is no longer necessary, you may leave these crutches behind.
Question: May I cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi through breath Buddha-recitation?
Answer: Yes. The Buddha-recitation samadhi aims at realizing the mind and seeing the nature (see in detail
Record of Groping at the Features of the Buddha-Recitation Samadhi

). For this, you should follow the breath Buddha-recitation method described above and attain one mind undisturbed. Then, on this foundation, cultivate the Buddha-recitation samadhi, in order to realize and enter the state of seeing the nature. The method is: while practicing breath Buddha-recitation, from the mysterious gate, turn the inner light down upon the lower dantian. If a false thought arises, it shows the inner light is scattered, not focused, not continuous. You should immediately bestir yourself and refocus the inner light, and the false thought will subside of itself. Practicing thus for a long time, when effort reaches its utmost and the practice becomes a pure, single whole, suddenly the thought of recitation falls away, and one realizes and enters the state of no-thought and yet no-thoughtlessness.
[The mysterious gate] Also called the upper dantian, located at the third eye (the heavenly eye).

[The lower dantian] This is the Guanyuan point of the Conception Vessel, located three cun below the navel (about four fingers' width), and is the place where the essence is stored. The lower dantian is the principal place for training, gathering, and storing the true qi. A person's primordial qi originates in the kidneys and is stored in the dantian, and by way of the three burners circulates throughout the body, driving the functional activity of the five organs and six viscera. The strength or weakness of the body, indeed life and death, all depend on the flourishing or decline of the dantian's primordial qi; therefore the care of the dantian's primordial qi is extremely important. When the dantian's primordial qi is full and vigorous, it can mobilize the body's potential and cause the true qi to circulate through the whole body. Fixing the attention on the dantian can regulate yin and yang, connect the heart and kidneys, make the true qi full, free the eight vessels, restore the prenatal physiological functions, and promote the body's health and longevity.

[Practicing thus for a long time] This is prajna perfuming ignorance; the moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya suddenly manifests. [When effort reaches its utmost and the practice becomes pure] The effort is used to the utmost, and the practice becomes a single, pure whole. [Suddenly] A description of openness and penetration; for example, 'suddenly open and bright,' 'suddenly penetrating and connected,' 'suddenly awakened.' 'Suddenly' also indicates the appearance of awakening; for example, the Family Instructions of Mr. Yan says: 'The years of obstruction and stagnation, suddenly dissolve like mist (the mist disperses).' Su Xun, in his First Letter to Inner-Han Ouyang, says: 'And after a long time, the more one reads it the finer it becomes, and in one's chest it is suddenly open and bright.' [The thought and the recitation fall away together] Both subject and object vanish, that is, the mind that recites and the Buddha that is recited fall away at the same time.
In cultivating the Buddha-recitation samadhi there are several points to note: first, it is best to have from the start some understanding of the true reality of all dharmas (see in detail
The True Reality of All Dharmas
article
) and of the original nature (see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha
article

); second, if any realms arise in the practice, one must neither receive nor cling to them, and only then can one advance; third, off the cushion one must refine the mind amid circumstances, not being turned by them, in order to truly realize the original nature.
Question: While investigating the Buddha-recitation, my false thoughts have grown far fewer, but when drowsiness overwhelms me, I am at a loss. How should I counteract the drowsiness?

Answer: You may counteract the drowsiness in this way. Bestir your spirit, and from time to time raise your head and look upward, and do deep abdominal breathing: inhale deeply through the nose (abdomen protruding), hold the breath for
second, then exhale slowly (abdomen sinking in), hold the breath for
second, and keep one cycle of inhalation and exhalation to about

seconds. At the same time, recite the Buddha-name and be clearly aware of the rising and falling of the abdomen. In this way the drowsiness will gradually disperse. Once the drowsiness has gone, return to your original way of reciting the Buddha-name.
